newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-HEAVYWEIGHT CLASH LOOMING FOR SAMPRAS, BECKER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HEAVYWEIGHT CLASH LOOMING FOR SAMPRAS, BECKER.

text.p: Pete Sampras and Boris Becker, Wimbledon's nearest equivalent to Evander Holyfield and Mike Tyson, are in no mood for fancy talk as they progress towards a major showdown at the All England Club this week.

The two champions, who share six Wimbledon singles titles between them, will face each other in the quarter-finals if they beat left-handers Petr Korda and Marcelo Rios respectively and neither shows any sign of taking a backward step.

Sampras steamrollered the unfortunate Byron Black of Zimbabwe 6-1 6-2 6-2 on Centre Court, while Becker completed an equally efficient demolition job on Britain's Mark Petchey 100 metres away on Court Number One.

The familiar rivals are the only two men left in the singles draw yet to drop a set, but are trying to maintain a low profile as the British press scramble to record the latest deeds of Tim Henman and Greg Rusedski.
"With Rusedski and Henman playing well, it's perfect. I prefer not being talked about and just playing my tennis," said Sampras, who required just 71 minutes to destroy Black.
"I prefer not being the centre of attention. I hope it doesn't change."
Sampras, nevertheless, was not shy of getting involved in discussions about the chewed-up nature of the famous Centre Court, already looking almost as battle-scarred as Holyfield's ear.

"I couldn't believe it in the warm-up....in the middle of the court there was no grass," said Sampras. "I've never seen Centre Court so chopped up... obviously it's because of the rain and all the play on it."
Under-foot conditions were better for Becker on the new showcourt, and he is currently sidestepping attention with practised ease.
"I came here not to be in the newspapers in the morning, but to play good tennis," said Becker. "I've been in the newspapers many times...it's fine with me."
The only thing which ruffled the German's composure after his 6-3 6-3 6-2 win over Petchey was the suggestion that Wimbledon was now the preserve of younger players.

"I strongly disagree. Especially at Wimbledon you need many things to survive a very strenuous two week tournament. You need to be very very patient. Your nerves have to be excellent. You need to know how to play on a grass court.

"My successes and those of Pete and a few others show it's very hard for young players to just come in and win it like (Gustavo) Kuerten did in Paris. I feel that's more likely to happen on clay than grass."

Becker's theory may yet be tested by one of his own compatriots after 19-year-old Nicolas Kiefer beat 13th seed Andrei Medvedev at 6-4 6-2 6-7 6-4 to reach the last 16 at Wimbledon at the first attempt.

Kiefer will be 20 the day before the men's final, but first has to find a way past third seed Yevgeny Kafelnikov, who finally shook off Australia's Jason Stoltenberg on his fifth match point to win 6-3 7-6 4-6 6-3.
The Czech Republic's Korda, seeded 16th, is another man intent on rewriting the script after battling back from 3-0 and 4-1 down in the final set to beat American Alex O'Brien 6-3 4-6 6-3 6-7 6-4.
"If Sampras wants to beat me he's going to have to play very well because I'm not going to give up, I'm going to fight. I don't think he likes playing against me."

Korda was distinctly unimpressed by the chill temperatures which have replaced the rain at this year's championships, while Rios, who reached the fourth round with a four-set win over John Van Lottum, is still finding the grass experience an alien one.

"I'm trying to adjust my game but at this stage, I can't help thinking that grass is better for the cows or playing a little golf or soccer on," smiled the Chilean ninth seed, fully aware of Becker's past record at Wimbledon. "I know his favourite surface is grass, but I'll be trying my best."
Meanwhile, three places in the last 16 will be filled by Australians after Pat Rafter and Todd Woodbridge joined compatriot Mark Woodforde in the fourth round.
Rafter beat Belgium's Christophe Van Garsse 7-5 6-4 4-6 6-3, and Woodbridge slipped past Germany's Alex Radulescu in straight sets.
